title: Smooth stabilizer of a semisimple tangent vector
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], with algebraic closure $\bar k$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $G$ be a smooth connected affine $k$-group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Put $\mathfrak g=T_{G/k,e}$ [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space], with commutator bracket [def-wf-lie-algebra]. The adjoint representation $\operatorname{Ad}:G\to\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)$ is the differential of conjugation, and $\operatorname{ad}(X)(Y)=[X,Y]$. Fix a closed group-scheme immersion $i:G\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$ [def-weil-closed-immersion, def-sc-general-linear-group], where $n\geq1$. Let $X\in\mathfrak g$ have $di(X)$ diagonalizable over $\bar k$. The functor on commutative $k$-algebras $$C_G(X)(A)=\{g\in G(A):\operatorname{Ad}(g)(X\otimes1)=X\otimes1\}$$ is represented by a smooth closed subgroup scheme $C\subseteq G$ [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Its tangent space, mapped into $\mathfrak g$, is exactly $$\operatorname{Lie}(C)=\{Y\in\mathfrak g:[Y,X]=0\}.$$ This assertion includes $X=0$, and assumes neither centrality of $X$ nor any characteristic restriction.

proof.text: Put $M=di(X)$ and $G=\operatorname{Spec}A$. The closed immersion into $\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$ presents $A$ as a quotient of $k[u_{ab},\det(u)^{-1}]$, by [def-sc-general-linear-group, def-weil-closed-immersion]; in particular it is a finite-type algebra. Write $U=(u_{ab})\in G(A)$ for the universal matrix and let $I\subseteq A$ be generated by the entries of $UM-MU$. Set $C=\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)$. The affine correspondence [def-weil-affine-spectrum] identifies its $R$-points, for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$, with the points $g\in G(R)$ for which $i(g)M=Mi(g)$. The quotient map makes $C\to G$ a closed immersion by [def-weil-closed-immersion].

source.place: Proposition 17.76, printed p.377: explicit equations for its stabilizer; the coordinate presentation is the general linear group definition.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-affine-group-dual-number-calculus], $di$ is injective and is compatible with adjoint actions. Its scalar extension to every $R$ remains injective: choose a $k$-linear left inverse on the matrix space by extending a basis of its image, and tensor that left inverse with $R$. The same calculus identifies the infinitesimal point belonging to $X\otimes1$ with $1+\delta M$, using the matrix tangent formula of [lem-sfb-affine-group-lie-tangent-calculus]. Therefore $\operatorname{Ad}(g)(X\otimes1)=X\otimes1$ is equivalent to $i(g)Mi(g)^{-1}=M$, and hence to the equations of step 1. This proves representability of the stated functor on all test algebras, including nonreduced ones.

source.place: Proposition 17.76, printed p.377; Sections 10.14 and 10.18--10.23, printed pp.190--193, for closed-subgroup tangent injectivity and adjoint functoriality.

proof.text: Matrices commuting with $M$ form a subgroup: $ghM=gMh=Mgh$, and $gM=Mg$ implies $g^{-1}M=Mg^{-1}$. Thus the identity, products and inverses of $C(R)$ remain in $C(R)$ for every $R$. To see the group operations as morphisms explicitly, put $B=A/I$. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], $C\times_kC=\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_kB)$. The two universal points over $B\otimes_kB$ commute with $M$, so their product defines an algebra map $A\to B\otimes_kB$ killing $I$. It factors through $B$ and defines multiplication on $C$ by [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. The inverse of the universal point over $B$ and the identity over $k$ give inverse and identity morphisms by the same factorization. The group diagrams commute because they do in $G$ and the maps $C(R)\to G(R)$ are injective. This is a closed subgroup in [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup].

source.place: Proposition 17.76, printed p.377, subgroup assertion; affine products are Stacks Tag 01I4, schemes.tex, lemma-fibre-product-affine-schemes.

proof.text: The infinitesimal point $t_X=E_{G,k}(X)$ supplied by [lem-sfb-affine-group-dual-number-calculus] belongs to $G(k[\delta])$, and its matrix is $1+\delta M$ by [lem-sfb-affine-group-lie-tangent-calculus]. Conjugation by this point is an automorphism of $G_{k[\delta]}$ reducing to the identity. Its coordinate map has the form $a\mapsto a+\delta D(a)$ for a $k$-linear map $D:A\to A$. Comparing coefficients in the multiplicative identity gives $D(ab)=aD(b)+D(a)b$. On the universal entries, $D(U)=MU-UM$, since $(1+\delta M)U(1-\delta M)=U+\delta(MU-UM)$. Determinant is invariant under conjugation, so $D(\det(U)^{-1})=0$. These entries and inverse determinant generate $A$; the product rule therefore implies $(D(a):a\in A)=I$. Infinitesimal conjugation was performed inside $G$, so this derivation is defined on its actual coordinate quotient, without an unverified stability assumption on its defining ideal.

source.place: Proposition 17.76, printed p.377: the infinitesimal-action modification of Lemma 13.6; Sections 10.18--10.23, printed pp.191--193.

proof.text: Extend scalars to $K=\bar k$. By the hypothesis choose $P\in\operatorname{GL}_n(K)$ with $P^{-1}MP=Z=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$, and put $V=P^{-1}UP$ in $A_K=A\otimes_kK$. The formula of step 4 gives $D_K(V_{ab})=(\lambda_a-\lambda_b)V_{ab}$ and $D_K(\det(V)^{-1})=0$. The $V_{ab}$ and $\det(V)^{-1}$ generate $A_K$ as a $K$-algebra: the inverse change is $U=PVP^{-1}$ and $\det V=\det U$. Every monomial in these generators is an eigenvector of $D_K$ by the product rule, with eigenvalue the sum of the generator eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity. Thus every element is a finite sum of eigenvectors. This sum is direct after grouping equal eigenvalues: on a finite set $F$ of distinct eigenvalues, the polynomial $\prod_{\mu\in F\setminus\{\lambda\}}(D_K-\mu)/(\lambda-\mu)$ projects a sum onto its $\lambda$ component, so a vanishing sum has all components zero. Consequently $A_K$ has exactly the eigenspace decomposition required by the derivation smoothness lemma. This uses no division by integers and allows eigenvalue sums to vanish in positive characteristic.

source.place: Proposition 17.76, printed p.377, modification of Lemma 13.6, printed p.256; explicit matrix-coordinate verification of semisimplicity supplied by the agent.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-semisimple-derivation-zero-smooth] to $A$ and the derivation $D$ of step 4. The algebra is finite type by step 1; its spectrum is the given smooth group $G$; step 5 proves geometric eigenspace decomposition; and step 4 identifies the derivation-value ideal with $I$. Every hypothesis of that lemma is therefore met. It gives smoothness over the original field $k$ of $\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)=C$, including for imperfect $k$.

source.place: Proposition 17.76, printed p.377: smoothness from the semisimple-derivation modification of Lemma 13.6, printed p.256.

proof.text: For $Y\in\mathfrak g$, the dual-number calculus identifies membership in the tangent space of the closed subgroup $C$ with membership of its infinitesimal point in $C(k[\epsilon])$. In the faithful representation that point is $1+\epsilon\,di(Y)$. Step 1's equations become $\epsilon(di(Y)M-Mdi(Y))=0$, equivalently $di(Y)M-Mdi(Y)=0$, since $k[\epsilon]$ is free on $1,\epsilon$. The bracket and functoriality clauses of [lem-sfb-affine-group-lie-tangent-calculus] identify this matrix commutator with $di([Y,X])$. Injectivity from [lem-sfb-affine-group-dual-number-calculus] makes its vanishing equivalent to $[Y,X]=0$. This proves the asserted equality as subspaces of $\mathfrak g$. If $X=0$, then $M=0$, $I=0$, $D=0$ and $C=G$, and the formula gives all of $\mathfrak g$, as required.
